The turn shifts the dispute from whether AI has harms at all to whether AI is beneficial only under governance and mitigation, making responsible deployment and guardrails the standard for judging whether it is good for society.

AG2 shifts the dispute from whether AI has benefits plus fixable harms to whether guardrails can actually keep up with AI’s harms in practice at scale, making feasibility of mitigation the decisive standard.

The turn shifts the dispute from a general claim that guardrails can mitigate harms to a new standard: whether AI governance can be made practical, enforceable, and proportionate to risk enough to steer deployment toward net social benefit.

It shifts the debate from a general pro/con assessment to a test of whether AI can be guided by enforceable access controls, continuous oversight, and selective restriction of high-risk uses, with net benefit remaining the relevant standard.

The turn shifts the debate from whether mitigations can fully stop harms to a new standard for being 'good for society': AI should be judged by whether it is used as decision support with human final authority, due process, and contestability in high-stakes settings.

The turn shifts the dispute from whether AI can be governed perfectly or whether current safeguards work, to a new standard of judging AI by a portfolio/allocative test: whether policy can expand low-risk high-benefit uses while pausing or restricting the highest-risk uses enough to yield net social benefit.

AG1 shifts the dispute from whether AI can be safely governed to whether 'good for society' should be judged by a broader net-benefit standard that includes AI’s ability to strengthen verification, misinformation defense, and learning, not just access and convenience.

The turn shifts the dispute to an opportunity-cost and evidence-based measurement standard: AI should be judged by whether targeted deployment yields demonstrably large benefits versus harms, rather than by a broad yes/no verdict on AI overall.

AG2 shifts the dispute to an opportunity-cost and substitutability test, arguing that AI is not socially good if its touted benefits can be met by safer alternatives and if the remaining platform harms still scale.

The turn shifts the dispute from whether AI’s harms can be mitigated in principle to whether mitigations are realistically achievable at the necessary scale and speed, making practical enforceability the decisive standard.

The turn shifts the dispute to a governance-based standard: AI should be judged by whether enforceable risk-management measures like pre-deployment evaluation, phased rollouts, accountability, and regulation can control harms, rather than by assuming governance failure and concluding net harm.

It shifts the dispute from whether governance is possible in general to whether AI can be safely judged and controlled by pre-deployment evaluation and phased rollout despite unpredictable emergent behavior at scale.

The turn shifts the dispute from whether monitoring can prevent harms to whether AI systems can be made socially acceptable through contestability and accountability procedures, introducing a new judging standard focused on appeal rights, explanations, and auditor access.

The turn shifts the dispute to a burden-of-proof/relative-baseline standard, arguing AI should be judged against realistic alternatives and that the harms must be shown to outweigh those alternatives rather than assuming failure of safeguards.

The turn shifts the debate from whether AI has net benefits and can be staged safely to a new judgment criterion: whether AI’s low-cost, large-scale misuse externalities and their speed of social propagation outweigh its localized benefits.

The turn shifts the dispute from whether detection can keep up after misuse to whether AI can be judged by the availability of upstream capability controls that reduce harmful generation and distribution at the source.

The turn shifts the debate to whether procurement and contract-based governance can actually address AI’s structural harms, introducing the criterion that governance must overcome incentive and information asymmetries rather than merely exist.
It shifts the dispute from whether AI is broadly good or bad to whether the key test is accountable deployment with safeguards and good transition policy, rather than treating harms as decisive.

AG2 shifts the debate from whether AI can be made beneficial with safeguards to the criterion that the key question is whether safeguards are reliably and evenly enforced in real deployments given incentives and power imbalances.

The turn shifts the dispute to a new judging standard: not whether safeguards can ever fail, but whether AI should be assessed by whether stronger enforceable governance can make benefits outweigh harms, comparable to other regulated technologies.

The turn shifts the dispute to a new standard for judging AI—whether deployment should be risk-tiered, phased, and reversible to manage irreversibility and enforcement lag, rather than simply whether safeguards exist or can be strengthened.

AG2 shifts the dispute to a net-effect criterion, arguing that the key question is whether the expected distribution of harms outweighs benefits in practice, rather than whether specific safeguards exist in theory.

AG2 shifts the dispute from whether AI can be governed well in principle to the criterion that governance must reliably work at scale under incentive pressure, and argues that because it cannot, the net societal effect is negative.

AG1 shifts the dispute from whether AI has risks to whether the right test is comparing AI’s harms against its ability to support defenses like misinformation detection, and limiting human review to high-stakes thresholds; this introduces a new criterion for judging social goodness based on managed deployment and countervailing protective uses.

It shifts the dispute to whether a holiday must be an effective standalone reform or can be justified as part of a package with other voting-access reforms, using that combined-policy standard to defend the holiday.

The turn shifts the dispute to whether Election Day provides a guaranteed paid time-and-pay entitlement for low-income workers, making reliability of wage/benefit protection the decisive standard rather than just whether the holiday offers more general scheduling flexibility.

It shifts the dispute from whether a holiday is the most reliable way to remove voting barriers to whether advancing a democratic-symbolic objective can justify the policy even without perfectly solving every scheduling constraint.
